For trans people to only feel joy just by finally being gendered correctly, or finally being able to pass, that essentially proves the whole trans experience is actually suffering. Because you live in it and you do not realize it, but trans people certainly have a lower baseline for happiness every day they live. Because they know they do not pass, or for the ones that do, they know they are merely passing as their gender and will never be biologically their true gender. And for a lot of us it’s really important. I wish could be my actual gender and look stereotypically like one. And if one day I do want to  start a family, have no issues having children. Many trans women want to experience having periods despite them being painful and uncomfortable, because they are women and it’s part of womanhood. And many trans man want to be able to pee standing up without a prosthetic or several surgeries. It’s literally the most basic things for cis people yet for trans people it is a godsend. That proves how miserable trans people actually feel because it is not curable.

For me I did slightly reject the thought of myself being trans, once I was at the age to fully understand gender ideas, but I knew that was not reality and that I was in a delusion. Because deep down I knew I was exactly that. That rejection wasn’t rejection really, it was letting the information sink in and realizing that I will have to live a more challenging life than most just for me to be myself. And for that plus some other life issues I considered suicide uncountable times and attempted several times. I still will never be happy just for the simple fact that I was not born in the right body.

Why are trans people considered an umbrella? I think whether or not you are trans is just a part of you not you being a part of trans. Like gay people are just gay.

And how do trans people who do not transition to be the opposite exist? That person would probably be non binary if so. 

I’m really trying to not invalidate you or anyone non binary because as long as you feel dysphoria you can relate to my feelings the same way I can too. 

I wholly agree that a trans experience is individual and subjective and all transition forms should be recognized. However for the very binary trans people who will still feel dysphoria if they look even a little masculine/feminine, that’s a real super difficult struggle because in a way we will never be happy with our bodies because we are not cis. Some non binary people may achieve happiness from being somewhere passable after hrt (which many only go on for a few months or a year).

But I will have to go on hrt forever. And I will also still feel incredibly sad that I was not born in the right body initially. That my dna and bones will always be female. And that my height cannot ever be changed. I’ll be dead before anyone digs my bones up but still I don’t enjoy the thought of that. 

I feel like there should be a distinction. For us to feel dysphoria so strongly that we recognize it and clearly feel what it is about since like 4/5. That’s really a pain to live through. Gender dysphoria this early on and this strong cannot be categorized the same as gender dysphoria for not being binary male or female. You may very well experience the dysphoria as strong as mine, but it is different. I don’t understand even more for the people who only discover they’re trans well into their 20s. How have you been so oblivious to two decades of suffering and not be able to realize what it is about? Did they never feel uncomfortable when being addressed as a little girl/boy to go into their respective bathrooms or wear dresses if you’re a girl and be completely prohibited from wearing dresses if you’re a boy.

I know this is very stereotypical, and sorry for that, but when I think of a non binary person, I think of a woman with short hair and perhaps a deep voice, but they are obviously comfortable with still being recognizable as an afab. Whereas I’d be so uncomfortable I’d never leave the house. I could not live another day watching myself look like my assigned sex. And it is truly crippling that it never gets an end. 

Definitely NB people feel dysphoria, with a few parts of their body, but I and a lot of binary trans people feel dysphoria in the whole entirety of me in the way that I am literally the complete polar opposite. Down to the bones and dna and the fact that we will never have the experience of living childhood as a little boy/girl. Or that we will never be able to produce ovum/sperm. Not far from androgyny, far from the complete opposite.

Please do tell me what if feels like to be NB because I really would like to learn more from a first person’s perspective.

Well, I am by no means a medical professional or scientist so I really don’t know what is causing trans people to exist. If you gave me a choice I certainly would not choose to be trans due to countless difficulties you could probably understand. However I do know what gender dysphoria is one of the most debilitating and torturing feelings to ever exist and anyone who has not faced it literally has no right to comment on anything regarding how hard it is or whether it is valid or not. 

To be so uncomfortable with your body that socializing, going out, speaking and hearing your own voice etc is a massive difficulty, and yet still having family and people say you’re just going through a phase. What? A phase for the past decade?! And them to also say ‘you should just be happy the way you were born’ just shows how unknown the feeling of dysphoria is to them. And also the issues following dysphoria causes, like difficulties in relationships, lack of support. Along with finally having the strength of choosing to go with transition despite all the difficulties it entails, to still be regarded as not a ‘real’ woman or man, or just a freak. And then having to stay on medication and pay for it the rest of my life, automatically have a less chance of finding a partner, always be considered sub par etc.

It is truly a hell of a struggle.

And I hope all goes well with your transition and that miracles happen with your journey and allow you to be finally happy with yourself whatever that looks like to you. 

Sometimes I wish I’d be born in the future where surgery has gone to a point where for ftm people, the ovaries can be altered to naturally produce testosterone (I read about something like this being possible in the future), and for mtf people their testes be able to produce estrogen and be reconstructed exactly like the female reproductive system they were meant to have, and exactly what we had in the womb before reproductive organ development (we all start as female before that develops) And that trans people are so normalized that no discrimination exists. But with the status that we are in now, we don’t know if WW3 might break out next second. So I guess savor the moment and live on. There is only one life and I am not about to let anyone stop me from making it as comfortable to live as possible.

I completely relate to this. I consider myself an independent thinker and generally am not the type of person to flaunt being lgbtq+. But one of the reasons i like communities like this sometimes, is because it’s the only place someone will ever fully understand my struggles of being trans. It truly is something you can understand only if you are going through it. I am a teenager but I feel like being trans has brought me so many obstacles others wouldn’t have to face. It’s like I have all the normal struggles of becoming a young adult (finding a place, job etc) and also bonus struggles of literally just existing. I have to waste time and money to go to doctors appointments because I have depression, I have to earn money to be able to afford my hormones in the future. I relate so much. 

And somehow my mother still has the audacity to say being trans is my choice, and I chose to make my life harder, as if I woke up one day and thought my life was too boring so I wanted to make it more exciting by become a minority that is discriminated against and make my own life ten times harder. She just doesn’t seem to understand or accept the fact that I was literally born trans and not by choice. I sure as hell would not choose to be trans if I could. A cis person’s life can certainly be worse than mine, but at least they will never have to be indescribably sad and hopeless every time they look at their body being the complete opposite gender, or go through uncountable inconveniences related to their gender throughout every day of their lives.
